**Common Statistics**

The formulas below are with the location parameter equal to zero and the scale parameter equal to one.

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\gamma$ |
| Mode | $\gamma - 1$ for $\gamma \ge 1$ |
| Range | 0 to $\infty$. |
| Standard Deviation | $\sqrt{\gamma}$ |
| Skewness | $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{\gamma}}$ |
| Kurtosis | $3 + \dfrac{6}{\gamma}$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}$ |

**Parameter Estimation**

The method of moments estimators of the 2-parameter gamma distribution are

$$\hat{\gamma} = \left(\frac{\bar{x}}{s}\right)^{2}$$

$$\hat{\beta} = \frac{s^{2}}{\bar{x}}$$

where $\bar{x}$ and $s$ are the sample mean and standard deviation, respectively.

The maximum likelihood estimates for the 2-parameter gamma distribution are the solutions of the following simultaneous equations

$$\hat{\beta} - \frac{\bar{x}}{\hat{\gamma}} = 0$$

$$\log{\hat{\gamma}} - \psi(\hat{\gamma}) - \log\left(\frac{\bar{x}}{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}{x_i}\right)^{1/n}}\right) = 0$$

with $\psi$ denoting the digamma function. These equations need to be solved numerically; this is typically accomplished by using statistical software packages.

**Software**

Some general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the gamma distribution.



##### Double Exponential Distribution {#sec-eda-double-exponential-distribution}

**Probability Density Function**

The general formula for the [probability density function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$f(x) = \frac{e^{-\left|\frac{x - \mu}{\beta}\right|}}{2\beta}$$

where $\mu$ is the [location parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters) and $\beta$ is the [scale parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters). The case where $\mu = 0$ and $\beta = 1$ is called the **standard double exponential distribution**. The equation for the standard double exponential distribution is

$$f(x) = \frac{e^{-|x|}}{2}$$

Since the general form of probability functions can be [expressed in terms of the standard distribution](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), all subsequent formulas in this section are given for the standard form of the function.

Note that the double exponential distribution is also commonly referred to as the Laplace distribution.

The following is the plot of the double exponential probability density function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

ddexp <- function(x) exp(-abs(x)) / 2

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = ddexp(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Standard double exponential probability density function](index_files/figure-html/fig-double-exponential-dist-pdf-1.png){#fig-double-exponential-dist-pdf width=672}
:::
:::


**Cumulative Distribution Function**

The formula for the [cumulative distribution function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$F(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{e^{x}}{2} & \text{for } x < 0 \\[4pt] 1 - \dfrac{e^{-x}}{2} & \text{for } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

The following is the plot of the double exponential cumulative distribution function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
pdexp <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0, exp(x) / 2, 1 - exp(-x) / 2)

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = pdexp(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "F(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Standard double exponential cumulative distribution function](index_files/figure-html/fig-double-exponential-dist-cdf-1.png){#fig-double-exponential-dist-cdf width=672}
:::
:::


**Percent Point Function**

The formula for the [percent point function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$G(p) = \begin{cases} \log(2p) & \text{for } p \le 0.5 \\ -\log(2(1 - p)) & \text{for } p > 0.5 \end{cases}$$

The following is the plot of the double exponential percent point function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
qdexp <- function(p) ifelse(p <= 0.5, log(2 * p), -log(2 * (1 - p)))

tibble(p = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(x = qdexp(p)) |>
  ggplot(aes(p, x)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = expression(alpha), y = expression(G(alpha))) +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Standard double exponential percent point function](index_files/figure-html/fig-double-exponential-dist-ppf-1.png){#fig-double-exponential-dist-ppf width=672}
:::
:::


**Hazard Function**

The formula for the [hazard function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$h(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{e^{x}}{2 - e^{x}} & \text{for } x < 0 \\[4pt] 1 & \text{for } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

The following is the plot of the double exponential hazard function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
hdexp <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0, exp(x) / (2 - exp(x)), 1)

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = hdexp(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "h(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Standard double exponential hazard function](index_files/figure-html/fig-double-exponential-dist-hazard-1.png){#fig-double-exponential-dist-hazard width=672}
:::
:::


**Cumulative Hazard Function**

The formula for the [cumulative hazard function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$H(x) = \begin{cases} -\log\!\left(1 - \dfrac{e^{x}}{2}\right) & \text{for } x < 0 \\[4pt] x + \log(2) & \text{for } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

The following is the plot of the double exponential cumulative hazard function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
hdexp_cum <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0, -log(1 - exp(x) / 2), x + log(2))

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = hdexp_cum(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "H(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

![Standard double exponential cumulative hazard function](index_files/figure-html/fig-double-exponential-dist-cumulative-hazard-1.png){#fig-double-exponential-dist-cumulative-hazard width=672}
:::
:::


**Survival Function**

The formula for the [survival function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$S(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - \dfrac{e^{x}}{2} & \text{for } x < 0 \\[4pt] \dfrac{e^{-x}}{2} & \text{for } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$$

The following is the plot of the double exponential survival function.


::: {.cell}


![Standard double exponential survival function](index_files/figure-html/fig-double-exponential-dist-survival-1.png){#fig-double-exponential-dist-survival width=672}
:::

**Inverse Survival Function**

The formula for the [inverse survival function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the double exponential distribution is

$$Z(p) = \begin{cases} \log(2(1 - p)) & \text{for } p \le 0.5 \\ -\log(2p) & \text{for } p > 0.5 \end{cases}$$

The following is the plot of the double exponential inverse survival function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
zdexp <- function(p) ifelse(p <= 0.5, log(2 * (1 - p)), -log(2 * p))

tibble(p = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(z = zdexp(p)) |>
  ggplot(aes(p, z)) +

  labs(x = expression(alpha), y = expression(Z(alpha))) +

```

**Common Statistics**

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\mu$ |
| Median | $\mu$ |
| Mode | $\mu$ |
| Range | $-\infty$ to $\infty$ |
| Standard Deviation | $\sqrt{2}\beta$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\sqrt{2}\left(\dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\right)$ |
| Skewness | 0 |
| Kurtosis | 6 |

**Parameter Estimation**

The maximum likelihood estimators of the location and scale parameters of the double exponential distribution are

$$\hat{\mu} = \tilde{X}$$

$$\hat{\beta} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}|X_{i} - \tilde{X}|}{N}$$

where $\tilde{X}$ is the sample median.

**Software**

Some general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the double exponential distribution.



##### Power Normal Distribution {#sec-eda-power-normal-distribution}

**Probability Density Function**

The formula for the [probability density function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the standard form of the power normal distribution is

$$f(x; p) = p\,\phi(x)\,(\Phi(-x))^{p - 1} \qquad x, p > 0$$

where $p$ is the [shape parameter](#sec-eda-families-of-distributions) (also referred to as the power parameter), $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the [standard normal](#sec-eda-normal-distribution) distribution, and $\phi$ is the probability density function of the [standard normal](#sec-eda-normal-distribution) distribution.

As with other probability distributions, the power normal distribution can be transformed with a [location parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), $\mu$, and a [scale parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), $\sigma$. We omit the equation for the general form of the power normal distribution. Since the general form of probability functions can be [expressed in terms of the standard distribution](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), all subsequent formulas in this section are given for the standard form of the function.

The following is the plot of the power normal probability density function with four values of $p$: 0.5, 1, 2, and 5.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

dpnorm <- function(x, p) p * dnorm(x) * (pnorm(-x))^(p - 1)

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  expand_grid(p = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5)) |>
  mutate(y = dpnorm(x, p),
         p = factor(p)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = p)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)", color = "p") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Power normal probability density function](index_files/figure-html/fig-power-normal-dist-pdf-1.png){#fig-power-normal-dist-pdf width=672}
:::
:::


**Cumulative Distribution Function**

The formula for the [cumulative distribution function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the power normal distribution is

$$F(x; p) = 1 - (\Phi(-x))^{p} \qquad x, p > 0$$

where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard [normal](#sec-eda-normal-distribution) distribution.

The following is the plot of the power normal cumulative distribution function with the same values of $p$ as the pdf plot above.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
ppnorm <- function(x, p) 1 - (pnorm(-x))^p

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
```

##### Power Lognormal Distribution {#sec-eda-power-lognormal-distribution}

**Probability Density Function**

The formula for the [probability density function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the standard form of the power lognormal distribution is

$$f(x; p, \sigma) = \left(\frac{p}{x\sigma}\right)\phi\!\left(\frac{\log x}{\sigma}\right)\left(\Phi\!\left(\frac{-\log x}{\sigma}\right)\right)^{p - 1} \qquad x, p, \sigma > 0$$

where $p$ (also referred to as the power parameter) and $\sigma$ are the [shape parameters](#sec-eda-families-of-distributions), $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the [standard normal](#sec-eda-normal-distribution) distribution, and $\phi$ is the probability density function of the [standard normal](#sec-eda-normal-distribution) distribution.

As with other probability distributions, the power lognormal distribution can be transformed with a [location parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), $\mu$, and a [scale parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), $B$. We omit the equation for the general form of the power lognormal distribution. Since the general form of probability functions can be [expressed in terms of the standard distribution](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), all subsequent formulas in this section are given for the standard form of the function.

The following is the plot of the power lognormal probability density function with four values of $p$ (0.5, 1, 2, and 5) and $\sigma$ set to 1.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

dplnorm <- function(x, p, sigma = 1) {
  (p / (x * sigma)) * dnorm(log(x) / sigma) * (pnorm(-log(x) / sigma))^(p - 1)
}

tibble(x = seq(0.01, 6, length.out = 401)) |>
  expand_grid(p = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5)) |>
  mutate(y = dplnorm(x, p),

  ggplot(aes(x, y, color = p)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)", color = "p") +
  theme_light()
```

##### Tukey-Lambda Distribution {#sec-eda-tukey-lambda-distribution}

**Probability Density Function**

The Tukey-Lambda density function does not have a simple, closed form. It is computed numerically.

The Tukey-Lambda distribution has the [shape parameter](#sec-eda-families-of-distributions) $\lambda$. As with other probability distributions, the Tukey-Lambda distribution can be transformed with a [location parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), $\mu$, and a [scale parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), $\sigma$. Since the general form of probability functions can be [expressed in terms of the standard distribution](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), all subsequent formulas in this section are given for the standard form of the function.

Because the source formula for the density is not given in closed form, no density plot is included here.

**Cumulative Distribution Function**

The Tukey-Lambda distribution does not have a simple, closed form for its cumulative distribution function. It is computed numerically.

Because the source formula for the cumulative distribution function is not given in closed form, no cumulative distribution function plot is included here.

**Percent Point Function**

The formula for the [percent point function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the standard form of the Tukey-Lambda distribution is

$$G(p; \lambda) = \frac{p^{\lambda} - (1 - p)^{\lambda}}{\lambda}$$

The following is the plot of the Tukey-Lambda percent point function. The source page illustrates this with four values of $\lambda$; here we use $\lambda = -1, 0, 0.14, 1$, which correspond respectively to distributions approximately Cauchy, exactly logistic, approximately normal, and exactly uniform (see **Comments** below). Since $\lambda = 0$ is a removable singularity in the formula above, that case is evaluated with its limiting form, $G(p; 0) = \log(p / (1 - p))$. Because the $\lambda = -1$ curve has very heavy (Cauchy-like) tails that would otherwise dwarf the other three curves, the plot's vertical range is restricted to $[-5, 5]$ for readability.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

qtukeylambda <- function(p, lambda) {
  if (lambda == 0) log(p / (1 - p)) else (p^lambda - (1 - p)^lambda) / lambda
}

tibble(p_prob = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 401)) |>
  expand_grid(lambda = c(-1, 0, 0.14, 1)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(x = qtukeylambda(p_prob, lambda)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(lambda = factor(lambda)) |>
  ggplot(aes(p_prob, x, color = lambda)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 5)) +
  labs(x = expression(alpha), y = expression(G(alpha)), color = expression(lambda)) +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Tukey-Lambda percent point function](index_files/figure-html/fig-tukey-lambda-dist-ppf-1.png){#fig-tukey-lambda-dist-ppf width=672}
:::
:::


**Other Probability Functions**

The Tukey-Lambda distribution is typically used to identify an appropriate distribution (see the comments below) and not used in statistical models directly. For this reason, we omit the formulas and plots for the hazard, cumulative hazard, survival, and inverse survival functions. We also omit the common statistics and parameter estimation sections.

**Comments**

The Tukey-Lambda distribution is actually a family of distributions that can approximate a number of common distributions. For example,

| $\lambda$ | Approximates |
|---|---|
| $\lambda = -1$ | approximately Cauchy |
| $\lambda = 0$ | exactly logistic |
| $\lambda = 0.14$ | approximately normal |
| $\lambda = 0.5$ | U-shaped |
| $\lambda = 1$ | exactly uniform (from -1 to +1) |

The most common use of this distribution is to generate a Tukey-Lambda PPCC plot of a data set. Based on the PPCC plot, an appropriate model for the data is suggested. For example, if the maximum correlation occurs for a value of $\lambda$ at or near 0.14, then the data can be modeled with a normal distribution. Values of $\lambda$ less than this imply a heavy-tailed distribution (with -1 approximating a Cauchy). That is, as the optimal value of $\lambda$ goes from 0.14 to -1, increasingly heavy tails are implied. Similarly, as the optimal value of $\lambda$ becomes greater than 0.14, shorter tails are implied.

As the Tukey-Lambda distribution is a symmetric distribution, the use of the Tukey-Lambda PPCC plot to determine a reasonable distribution to model the data only applies to symmetric distributions. A histogram of the data should provide evidence as to whether the data can be reasonably modeled with a symmetric distribution.

**Software**

Most general purpose statistical software programs do not support the probability functions for the Tukey-Lambda distribution.



##### Extreme Value Type I Distribution {#sec-eda-extreme-value-type-i-distribution}

**Probability Density Function**

The extreme value type I distribution has two forms. One is based on the smallest extreme and the other is based on the largest extreme. We call these the minimum and maximum cases, respectively. Formulas and plots for both cases are given. The extreme value type I distribution is also referred to as the **Gumbel distribution**.

The general formula for the [probability density function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the Gumbel (minimum) distribution is

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\beta} e^{\frac{x - \mu}{\beta}} e^{-e^{\frac{x - \mu}{\beta}}}$$

where $\mu$ is the [location parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters) and $\beta$ is the [scale parameter](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters). The case where $\mu = 0$ and $\beta = 1$ is called the **standard Gumbel distribution**. The equation for the standard Gumbel distribution (minimum) reduces to

$$f(x) = e^{x} e^{-e^{x}}$$

The general formula for the probability density function of the Gumbel (maximum) distribution is

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\beta} e^{-\frac{x - \mu}{\beta}} e^{-e^{-\frac{x - \mu}{\beta}}}$$

where $\mu$ is the location parameter and $\beta$ is the scale parameter. The case where $\mu = 0$ and $\beta = 1$ is called the standard Gumbel distribution. The equation for the standard Gumbel distribution (maximum) reduces to

$$f(x) = e^{-x} e^{-e^{-x}}$$

Since the general form of probability functions can be [expressed in terms of the standard distribution](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), all subsequent formulas in this section are given for the standard form of the function. R does not provide built-in `d`/`p`/`q` functions for the Gumbel distribution, so the closed-form expressions above are implemented directly below.

The following is the plot of the standard Gumbel probability density function for the minimum case.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
dgumbel_min <- function(x) exp(x) * exp(-exp(x))

tibble(x = seq(-8, 3, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = dgumbel_min(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

**Common Statistics**

The formulas below are for the maximum order statistic case.

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\mu + 0.5772\beta$ (the constant 0.5772 is Euler's number) |
| Median | $\mu - \beta\ln(\ln(2))$ |
| Mode | $\mu$ |
| Range | $-\infty$ to $\infty$ |
| Standard Deviation | $\dfrac{\beta\pi}{\sqrt{6}}$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\dfrac{\beta\pi}{\sqrt{6}(\mu + 0.5772\beta)}$ |
| Skewness | 1.13955 |
| Kurtosis | 5.4 |

**Parameter Estimation**

The method of moments estimators of the Gumbel (maximum) distribution are

$$\tilde{\beta} = \frac{s\sqrt{6}}{\pi}$$
$$\tilde{\mu} = \bar{X} - 0.5772\tilde{\beta} = \bar{X} - 0.45006s$$

where $\bar{X}$ and $s$ are the sample mean and standard deviation, respectively.

The method of moments estimators of the Gumbel (minimum) distribution are

$$\tilde{\beta} = \frac{s\sqrt{6}}{\pi}$$
$$\tilde{\mu} = \bar{X} + 0.5772\tilde{\beta} = \bar{X} + 0.45006s$$

where $\bar{X}$ and $s$ are the sample mean and standard deviation, respectively.

The maximum likelihood estimates for the maximum case are the solution to the following simultaneous equations

$$\bar{x} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{x_i \exp(-x_i/\hat{\beta})}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\exp(-x_i/\hat{\beta})}} - \hat{\beta} = 0$$
$$-\hat{\beta} \log\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\exp(-x_i/\hat{\beta})}\right) - \hat{\mu} = 0$$

For the minimum case, replace $-x_i$ with $x_i$ in the above equations.

These equations need to be solved numerically and this is typically accomplished by using statistical software packages.

**Software**

Some general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the extreme value type I distribution.



##### Beta Distribution {#sec-eda-beta-distribution}

**Probability Density Function**

The general formula for the [probability density function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the beta distribution is

$$f(x) = \frac{(x - a)^{p-1}(b - x)^{q-1}}{B(p,q)(b-a)^{p+q-1}} \;\;\;\;\;\;\; a \le x \le b;\; p, q > 0$$

where $p$ and $q$ are the [shape parameters](#sec-eda-families-of-distributions), $a$ and $b$ are the lower and upper bounds, respectively, of the distribution, and $B(p,q)$ is the beta function. The beta function has the formula

$$B(\alpha,\beta) = \int_{0}^{1}{t^{\alpha-1}(1 - t)^{\beta-1}dt}$$

The case where $a = 0$ and $b = 1$ is called the **standard beta distribution**. The equation for the standard beta distribution is

$$f(x) = \frac{x^{p-1}(1-x)^{q-1}}{B(p,q)} \;\;\;\;\;\;\; 0 \le x \le 1;\; p, q > 0$$

Typically we define the general form of a distribution in terms of [location and scale parameters](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters). The beta is different in that we define the general distribution in terms of the lower and upper bounds. However, the location and scale parameters can be defined in terms of the lower and upper limits as follows:

$$\text{location} = a$$
$$\text{scale} = b - a$$

Since the general form of probability functions can be [expressed in terms of the standard distribution](#sec-eda-location-and-scale-parameters), all subsequent formulas in this section are given for the standard form of the function.

The beta distribution has two shape parameters and no single choice is illustrative of every shape it can take; the source page shows four combinations. Here the shape parameters $p = 2$ and $q = 3$ are used for the plots below, chosen because they produce a clearly non-uniform, non-symmetric density on $[0, 1]$ (base R's `dbeta`/`pbeta`/`qbeta` use the arguments `shape1` and `shape2` for $p$ and $q$, respectively).

The following is the plot of the beta probability density function for $p = 2$, $q = 3$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

tibble(x = seq(0, 1, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = dbeta(x, shape1 = 2, shape2 = 3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Beta probability density function (shape1 = 2, shape2 = 3)](index_files/figure-html/fig-beta-dist-pdf-1.png){#fig-beta-dist-pdf width=672}
:::
:::


**Cumulative Distribution Function**

The formula for the [cumulative distribution function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) of the beta distribution is also called the incomplete beta function ratio (commonly denoted by $I_x$) and is defined as

$$F(x) = I_{x}(p,q) = \frac{\int_{0}^{x}{t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}dt}}{B(p,q)} \;\;\;\;\;\;\; 0 \le x \le 1;\; p, q > 0$$

where $B$ is the beta function defined above.

The following is the plot of the beta cumulative distribution function for the same shape parameters as the pdf plot above.

**Other Probability Functions**

Since the beta distribution is not typically used for reliability applications, the hazard, cumulative hazard, survival, and inverse survival probability functions are omitted here, following the source page.

**Common Statistics**

The formulas below are for the case where the lower limit is zero and the upper limit is one.

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\dfrac{p}{p+q}$ |
| Mode | $\dfrac{p-1}{p+q-2} \;\;\;\;\; p, q > 1$ |
| Range | 0 to 1 |
| Standard Deviation | $\sqrt{\dfrac{pq}{(p+q)^{2}(p+q+1)}}$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\sqrt{\dfrac{q}{p(p+q+1)}}$ |
| Skewness | $\dfrac{2(q-p)\sqrt{p+q+1}}{(p+q+2)\sqrt{pq}}$ |

**Parameter Estimation**

First consider the case where $a$ and $b$ are assumed to be known. For this case, the method of moments estimates are

$$p = \bar{x}\left(\frac{\bar{x}(1-\bar{x})}{s^{2}} - 1\right)$$
$$q = (1 - \bar{x})\left(\frac{\bar{x}(1-\bar{x})}{s^{2}} - 1\right)$$

where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean and $s^2$ is the sample variance. If $a$ and $b$ are not 0 and 1, respectively, then replace $\bar{x}$ with $\dfrac{\bar{x} - a}{b-a}$ and $s^2$ with $\dfrac{s^2}{(b-a)^2}$ in the above equations.

For the case when $a$ and $b$ are known, the maximum likelihood estimates can be obtained by solving the following set of equations

$$\psi(\hat{p}) - \psi(\hat{p} + \hat{q}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\log\left(\frac{Y_i - a}{b - a}\right)}$$
$$\psi(\hat{q}) - \psi(\hat{p} + \hat{q}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\log\left(\frac{b - Y_i}{b - a}\right)}$$

Maximum likelihood estimation for the case when $a$ and $b$ are not known can sometimes be problematic. Chapter 14 of Bury<!-- XREF: Bury reference for beta distribution moment/maximum-likelihood estimation with unknown bounds; source handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm --> discusses both moment and maximum likelihood estimation for this case.

**Software**

Most general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the beta distribution.



##### Binomial Distribution {#sec-eda-binomial-distribution}

**Probability Mass Function**

The binomial distribution is used when there are exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes of a trial. These outcomes are appropriately labeled "success" and "failure". The binomial distribution is used to obtain the probability of observing $x$ successes in $N$ trials, with the probability of success on a single trial denoted by $p$. The binomial distribution assumes that $p$ is fixed for all trials.

The formula for the binomial probability mass function is

$$P(x;p,n) = \binom{n}{x} (p)^{x}(1-p)^{(n-x)} \;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n$$

where

$$\binom{n}{x} = \frac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}$$

The binomial distribution is discrete, defined only at the integers $x = 0, 1, \ldots, n$, so the plots below use `geom_col()` rather than a connected line to avoid implying that the probability mass exists between integers.

The following is the plot of the binomial probability mass function for $n = 100$ and 4 different values of $p$: 0.1, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

ps <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75)

crossing(x = 0:100, p = ps) |>
  mutate(
    y = dbinom(x, size = 100, prob = p),
    p_label = paste("p =", p),
    p_label = fct_reorder(p_label, p)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~p_label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "P(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Binomial probability mass function for four values of p (n = 100)](index_files/figure-html/fig-binomial-dist-pmf-1.png){#fig-binomial-dist-pmf width=672}
:::
:::


**Cumulative Distribution Function**

The formula for the binomial cumulative probability function is

$$F(x;p,n) = \sum_{i=0}^{x}{\binom{n}{i}(p)^{i}(1-p)^{(n-i)}}$$

Because the binomial distribution is discrete, its cumulative distribution function is a right-continuous step function, so the plot below uses `geom_step()`.

The following is the plot of the binomial cumulative distribution function for the same values of $n$ and $p$ as the pmf plot above.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_step() +
  facet_wrap(~p_label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "F(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

The binomial percent point function does not exist in simple closed form. It is computed numerically. Note that because this is a discrete distribution that is only defined for integer values of $x$, the percent point function is not smooth in the way the percent point function typically is for a continuous distribution.

The following is the plot of the binomial percent point function for the same values of $n$ and $p$ as the pmf plot above.

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $np$ |
| Mode | $p(n+1) - 1 \le x \le p(n+1)$ |
| Range | 0 to $n$ |
| Standard Deviation | $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\sqrt{\dfrac{(1-p)}{np}}$ |
| Skewness | $\dfrac{(1-2p)}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}$ |
| Kurtosis | $3 - \dfrac{6}{n} + \dfrac{1}{np(1-p)}$ |

**Comments**

The binomial distribution is probably the most commonly used discrete distribution.

**Parameter Estimation**

The maximum likelihood estimator of $p$ (for fixed $n$) is

$$\tilde{p} = \frac{x}{n}$$

**Software**

Most general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the binomial distribution.



##### Poisson Distribution {#sec-eda-poisson-distribution}

**Probability Mass Function**

The Poisson distribution is used to model the number of events occurring within a given time interval.

The formula for the Poisson probability mass function is

$$p(x;\lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x}}{x!} \;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

$\lambda$ is the [shape parameter](#sec-eda-families-of-distributions) which indicates the average number of events in the given time interval.

The Poisson distribution is discrete, defined only at the non-negative integers, so the plots below use `geom_col()` rather than a connected line to avoid implying that probability mass exists between integers.

The following is the plot of the Poisson probability mass function for 4 different values of $\lambda$: 5, 15, 25, and 35.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
lambdas <- c(5, 15, 25, 35)

crossing(x = 0:50, lambda = lambdas) |>
  mutate(
    y = dpois(x, lambda = lambda),
    lambda_label = paste("lambda =", lambda),
    lambda_label = fct_reorder(lambda_label, lambda)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~lambda_label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "p(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

The formula for the Poisson cumulative probability function is

$$F(x;\lambda) = \sum_{i=0}^{x}{\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{i}}{i!}}$$

**Common Statistics**

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\lambda$ |
| Mode | For non-integer $\lambda$, the largest integer less than $\lambda$. For integer $\lambda$, $x = \lambda$ and $x = \lambda - 1$ are both the mode. |
| Range | 0 to $\infty$ |
| Standard Deviation | $\sqrt{\lambda}$ |
| Coefficient of Variation | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ |
| Skewness | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ |
| Kurtosis | $3 + \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$ |

**Parameter Estimation**

The maximum likelihood estimator of $\lambda$ is

$$\tilde{\lambda} = \bar{X}$$

where $\bar{X}$ is the sample mean.

**Software**

Most general purpose statistical software programs support at least some of the probability functions for the Poisson distribution.



#### Tables for Probability Distributions {#sec-eda-367}

Several commonly used tables for probability distributions can be referenced below.

The values from these tables can also be obtained from most general purpose statistical software programs (in R, via the `qnorm()`, `qt()`, `qf()`, and `qchisq()` functions used to generate them here). Most introductory statistics textbooks (e.g., Snedecor and Cochran<!-- XREF: EDA bibliography entry for Snedecor and Cochran; source handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm#Snedecor -->) contain more extensive tables than are included here. ##### Cumulative Distribution Function of the Standard Normal Distribution {#sec-eda-standard-normal-cdf-table}

The table below contains the area under the standard normal curve from 0 to $z$. This can be used to compute the [cumulative distribution function](#sec-eda-related-distributions) values for the [standard normal distribution](#sec-eda-normal-distribution).

The table utilizes the symmetry of the normal distribution, so what is in fact given is $P[0 \le x \le |a|]$, where $a$ is the value of interest. This is demonstrated in the graph below for $a = 0.5$. The shaded area of the curve represents the probability that $x$ is between 0 and $a$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

a <- 0.5

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = dnorm(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x >= 0, x <= a),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Standard normal PDF with shaded area between 0 and a = 0.5](index_files/figure-html/fig-standard-normal-cdf-table-shaded-1.png){#fig-standard-normal-cdf-table-shaded width=672}
:::
:::


This can be clarified by a few simple examples.

1. What is the probability that $x$ is less than or equal to 1.53? Look for 1.5 in the X column, go right to the 0.03 column to find the value 0.43699. Now add 0.5 (for the probability less than zero) to obtain the final result of 0.93699.
2. What is the probability that $x$ is less than or equal to -1.53? For negative values, use the relationship $P[x \le a] = 1 - P[x \le |a|]$ for $x < 0$. From the first example, this gives $1 - 0.93699 = 0.06301$.
3. What is the probability that $x$ is between -1 and 0.5? Look up the values for 0.5 ($0.5 + 0.19146 = 0.69146$) and -1 ($1 - (0.5 + 0.34134) = 0.15866$). Then subtract the results ($0.69146 - 0.15866$) to obtain the result $0.5328$.

To use this table with a non-standard normal distribution (either the location parameter is not 0 or the scale parameter is not 1), standardize your value by subtracting the mean and dividing the result by the standard deviation. Then look up the value for this standardized value.

##### Upper Critical Values of the Student's t Distribution {#sec-eda-t-distribution-table}

This table contains critical values of the [Student's t distribution](#sec-eda-t-distribution) computed using the [cumulative distribution function](#sec-eda-related-distributions). The t distribution is symmetric so that $t_{1-\alpha,\nu} = -t_{\alpha,\nu}$.

The t table can be used for both one-sided (lower and upper) and two-sided tests using the appropriate value of $\alpha$.

The significance level, $\alpha$, is demonstrated in the graph below, which displays a t distribution with 10 degrees of freedom. The most commonly used significance level is $\alpha = 0.05$. For a two-sided test, we compute $1 - \alpha/2$, or $1 - 0.05/2 = 0.975$ when $\alpha = 0.05$. If the absolute value of the test statistic is greater than the critical value (0.975), then we reject the null hypothesis. Due to the symmetry of the t distribution, we only tabulate the positive critical values in the table below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

df <- 10
crit <- qt(0.975, df)

tibble(x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = dt(x, df)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x >= crit),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x <= -crit),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Two-sided test for alpha = 0.05 (t distribution, 10 df)](index_files/figure-html/fig-t-distribution-table-shaded-1.png){#fig-t-distribution-table-shaded width=672}
:::
:::


Given a specified value for $\alpha$:

1. For a two-sided test, find the column corresponding to $1 - \alpha/2$ and reject the null hypothesis if the absolute value of the test statistic is greater than the value of $t_{1-\alpha/2,\nu}$ in the table below.
2. For an upper, one-sided test, find the column corresponding to $1 - \alpha$ and reject the null hypothesis if the test statistic is greater than the table value.
3. For a lower, one-sided test, find the column corresponding to $1 - \alpha$ and reject the null hypothesis if the test statistic is less than the negative of the table value.

##### Upper Critical Values of the F Distribution {#sec-eda-f-distribution-table}

This table contains the upper critical values of the [F distribution](#sec-eda-f-distribution). This table is used for one-sided F tests at the $\alpha$ = 0.05, 0.10, and 0.01 levels.

More specifically, a test statistic is computed with $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ degrees of freedom, and the result is compared to this table. For a one-sided test, the null hypothesis is rejected when the test statistic is greater than the tabled value. This is demonstrated with the graph of an F distribution with $\nu_1 = 10$ and $\nu_2 = 10$. The shaded area of the graph indicates the rejection region at the $\alpha$ significance level. Since this is a one-sided test, we have $\alpha$ probability in the upper tail of exceeding the critical value and zero in the lower tail. Because the F distribution is asymmetric, a two-sided test requires a set of tables (not included here) that contain the rejection regions for both the lower and upper tails.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

df1 <- 10
df2 <- 10
crit <- qf(0.95, df1, df2)

tibble(x = seq(0.001, 5, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = df(x, df1, df2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x >= crit),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

##### Critical Values of the Chi-Square Distribution {#sec-eda-chi-square-distribution-table}

This table contains the critical values of the [chi-square distribution](#sec-eda-chi-square-distribution). Because of the lack of symmetry of the chi-square distribution, separate tables are provided for the upper and lower tails of the distribution.

A test statistic with $\nu$ degrees of freedom is computed from the data. For upper-tail one-sided tests, the test statistic is compared with a value from the table of upper-tail critical values. For two-sided tests, the test statistic is compared with values from both the table for the upper-tail critical values and the table for the lower-tail critical values.

The significance level, $\alpha$, is demonstrated with the graph below which shows a chi-square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom for a two-sided test at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. If the test statistic is greater than the upper-tail critical value or less than the lower-tail critical value, we reject the null hypothesis. Specific instructions are given below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)

df <- 3
upper_crit <- qchisq(0.975, df)
lower_crit <- qchisq(0.025, df)

tibble(x = seq(0.001, 12, length.out = 401)) |>
  mutate(y = dchisq(x, df)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x >= upper_crit),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = ~ filter(.x, x <= lower_crit),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)") +
  theme_light()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Two-sided test for alpha = 0.05 (chi-square distribution, 3 df)](index_files/figure-html/fig-chi-square-distribution-table-shaded-1.png){#fig-chi-square-distribution-table-shaded width=672}
:::
:::


Given a specified value of $\alpha$:

1. For a two-sided test, find the column corresponding to $1 - \alpha/2$ in the table for upper-tail critical values and reject the null hypothesis if the test statistic is greater than the tabled value. Similarly, find the column corresponding to $\alpha/2$ in the table for lower-tail critical values and reject the null hypothesis if the test statistic is less than the tabled value.
2. For an upper-tail one-sided test, find the column corresponding to $1 - \alpha$ in the table containing upper-tail critical values and reject the null hypothesis if the test statistic is greater than the tabled value.
3. For a lower-tail one-sided test, find the column corresponding to $\alpha$ in the lower-tail critical values table and reject the null hypothesis if the computed test statistic is less than the tabled value.

##### Critical Values of the t* Distribution {#sec-eda-t-star-distribution-table}

A test statistic with $\nu$ degrees of freedom is compared with the critical value. If the absolute value of the test statistic exceeds the tabled value, the calibration of the instrument is judged to be out of control.

Unlike the other tables in this section, the t* distribution has no simple closed-form generating function — the values below were determined by NIST from simulation studies specific to this calibration application, so they are reproduced here directly from the original table rather than computed from an R distribution function.

##### Critical Values of the Normal PPCC Distribution {#sec-eda-normal-ppcc-distribution-table}

This table contains the critical values of the normal probability plot correlation coefficient (PPCC) distribution that are appropriate for determining whether or not a data set came from a population with approximately a [normal distribution](#sec-eda-normal-distribution). It is used in conjunction with a [normal probability plot](#sec-eda-normal-probability-plot). The test statistic is the correlation coefficient of the points that make up a normal probability plot. This test statistic is compared with the critical value below. If the test statistic is less than the tabulated value, the null hypothesis that the data came from a population with a normal distribution is rejected.

For example, suppose a set of 50 data points had a correlation coefficient of 0.985 from the normal probability plot. At the 5% significance level, the critical value is 0.9761. Since 0.985 is greater than 0.9761, we cannot reject the null hypothesis that the data came from a population with a normal distribution.

Since perfect normality implies perfect correlation (i.e., a correlation value of 1), we are only interested in rejecting normality for correlation values that are too low. That is, this is a lower one-tailed test.

The values in this table were determined from simulation studies by Filliben and Devaney<!-- XREF: EDA bibliography entries for Filliben (PPCC) and Devaney; source handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm#PPCC and handbook/eda/section4/eda43.htm#Devaney -->. Like the [t* distribution table](#sec-eda-t-star-distribution-table), these values have no simple closed-form generating function, so they are reproduced here directly from the original table rather than computed from an R distribution function.
